papers.title: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction for Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) for anxiety symptoms in adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Data Sources: CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, SocINDEX, ERIC (EBSCO), and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global were searched from inception to October 2025; identified trial protocols were hand-searched for subsequent reports through February 2026. Eligibility criteria for selecting studies: Randomized, non-randomized, and single-arm trials evaluating the effects of MBSR on anxiety in adults with GAD. Data extraction and synthesis: Two authors independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. The primary outcome was anxiety symptoms; the secondary outcome was adverse events. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted, and certainty of evidence was assessed. Results: Of 19 included reports (16 independent samples), 8 randomized controlled trials (n=1,012) were included in the primary meta-analysis. MBSR significantly reduced anxiety symptoms vs. waitlist (Hedges' g=-0.88; 95% CI -1.57 to -0.19) and general active comparators (g=-0.85; 95% CI -1.15 to -0.54), and showed no significant difference vs. escitalopram in two linked trials (g=0.09; 95% CI -0.11 to 0.29), with fewer adverse events in the in-person trial, the only one reporting them (15% vs. 79%; number needed to treat to avoid harm=2). GRADE certainty of evidence was high for the escitalopram comparison and very low for waitlist. Conclusions: MBSR is a well-tolerated, nonpharmacologic treatment option for adults with GAD. Anxiety reductions were similar to escitalopram, with fewer adverse events; independent replication is needed. MBSR may be a viable option for patients who prefer non-pharmacological management or who cannot tolerate medication. Systematic review registration: PROSPERO CRD420251140213.

papers.title: Early-Life Environmental Exposures and Brain Structure in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Background: Schizophrenia is widely considered a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by premorbid alterations in brain structure. Urban upbringing is a well-established environmental risk factor. However, urbanicity is often operationalised using broad population-based measures, leaving unclear which features of urban environments might affect the developing brain. This gap limits progress in understanding the pathways linking urban upbringing to schizophrenia, an increasingly important question as global urbanisation progresses. Cortical gyrification is especially informative in this context, as it is largely established before birth and remains relatively stable thereafter, offering a promising retrospective marker of early-life neurodevelopmental disturbances. Study Design: In this case-control MRI study, we examined whether residential environmental exposures at birth were associated with adult brain structure in 51 individuals with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and 88 healthy controls matched for age, sex and socioeconomic status. Birth addresses were linked to geospatial measures of air pollution, green space, built volume, built surface and population density. Study Results: Higher air pollution at birth was associated with lower cortical gyrification in individuals with schizophrenia, but not in healthy controls, particularly in orbitofrontal and inferior frontal regions. No comparable associations were observed for grey matter volume, cortical thickness or surface area. Conclusions: These findings suggest that air pollution at birth may be linked to hypogyria in schizophrenia and provide a potential bridge between epidemiological research on urbanicity and neurodevelopmental models of schizophrenia. In turn, this work provides a critical starting point for future work assessing how early urban environments become biologically embedded in schizophrenia risk.

papers.title: Protocol for: Diagnostic trajectories of patients receiving unspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses. A retrospective, longitudinal, register-based study in a large UK secondary mental healthcare service from 2007 to 2024
papers.abstract: Background Unspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses (ICD code F29) are commonly used when the underlying disorder remains uncertain, particularly at first presentation. These diagnoses may persist or later be revised as the clinical picture evolves, yet little is known about their long-term trajectories or implications for treatment and service use in routine mental healthcare. Objectives To describe the usage and persistence of unspecified non-organic psychosis (F29) and other non-specific diagnoses, and the time to transition to a specific diagnosis. Secondary objectives are to describe temporal trends in their use, identify demographic and clinical characteristics associated with diagnostic persistence, and characterise treatment patterns, service utilisation, mortality, and discharge across diagnostic groups. Methods We will conduct a retrospective longitudinal cohort study using de-identified electronic health-record data from the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (SLaM), accessed through the Clinical Record Interactive Search (CRIS) system, between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2024. The study population will include patients with an ICD-10 psychosis-spectrum diagnosis (F2x.x), substance induced psychotic disorder (or F1x.5), bipolar disorder or affective disorder with documented psychotic symptoms(F32/3.3). Diagnoses will be classified as specific or non-specific according to their ICD-10 category. Primary analysis will examine time from first F29 diagnosis to first subsequent specific psychosis-spectrum or bipolar diagnosis using Cox proportional hazards regression, with discharge from SLaM, death and administrative end of follow-up treated as censoring events. Associations with diagnostic transition will be examined adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, area-level deprivation, route of service entry, and calendar period. Secondary competing-risk analysis will estimate the cumulative incidence of diagnostic transition using the Aalen Johansen estimator, treating discharge and death as competing events. Ethics and Dissemination CRIS operates under ethical approval from the South Central Oxford C Research Ethics Committee (23/SC/0257). Project-specific approval was received from the CRIS Oversight Committee as Project 23 095. The study will be reported in accordance with the RECORD extension of the STROBE guidelines. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication and will provide evidence on the longitudinal use and refinement of non-specific psychosis-spectrum diagnoses in routine secondary mental healthcare.

papers.title: Developmental trajectories of child resilience, their determinants, and associations with risk experiences and behaviours: protocol for a national cohort study within the ReDiKid project
papers.abstract: Background: Resilience during the transition from middle childhood towards early adolescence is best understood as a dynamic, adversity-activated developmental process rather than a fixed individual trait. Building on the Resilient Kid in the Digital World framework, this protocol describes the longitudinal component of the broader research programme, designed to characterise developmental trajectories of resilience-related capacities and resources and adaptive functioning, identify their determinants, and examine prospective associations with risk experiences and behaviours across behavioural, family, school, and digital contexts. Methods: This is a national school-based cohort study following children aged 9-11 years at baseline across four waves at approximately six-month intervals from autumn 2025 to spring 2027. Schools are selected from the Czech national register using stratified probability-proportional-to-size sampling by region, municipality status, and area-level socioeconomic status; all eligible Grade 4 and Grade 5 pupils in participating schools are invited. The recruitment plan covers approximately 72 schools and 8,000 eligible children, with an anticipated 50-60% participation rate for complete child-parent pairs, corresponding to a target of approximately 4,000-4,800 linked child-parent dyads at baseline. Longitudinal planning aims to retain at least 1,000 linked dyads through Wave 4. Data are collected through child self-report, parent self- and proxy-report, and school-coordinator online questionnaires. Measures cover resilience-related capacities and resources, adaptive functioning and well-being, risk exposures, digital engagement, health-related behaviours, family context, parental mediation, and school context. Analyses will be tailored to the specific research questions and may include longitudinal and multilevel approaches complemented by reciprocal and person-oriented analyses. Discussion: The study provides a multi-dimensional, nationally distributed longitudinal resource for examining how child functioning and resilience-related resources change together with risk experiences and contextual conditions during a key developmental transition. The design explicitly distinguishes resilience-related measures from evidence of resilience under adversity and treats digital environments as one interacting developmental context rather than as an isolated exposure domain. The cohort may also inform understanding of early vulnerability and protective processes relevant to problematic digital engagement, without treating such indicators as clinical diagnoses.

papers.title: Prevalence of DSM-5 eating disorders and associated impairment and service use among children and young people in England: analysis of a general population survey
papers.abstract: Background: Eating disorders (EDs) typically emerge in adolescence and carry substantial morbidity. DSM-5 revised EDs classification, introducing Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (OSFED) and Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID). We estimated general population prevalence of EDs, including ARFID, in children and young people (CYP), and the associated impairment, which remains poorly characterised. Methods: We analysed the Mental Health of Children and Young People in England (MHCYP) 2023 survey, a nationally representative probability sample. All participants were screened for possible eating problems. Screen positives and a random sample of screen negatives were invited to a second-stage assessment; giving an analytic sample of 1,738 aged 11-25 years. Associations with impairment, mental health difficulties and service use were estimated using survey-weighted regression adjusted for age and sex. Results: Any ED affected 6.7% (95% CI 5.4-8.3) of 11-25-year-olds and was over three times more common in females (10.7%) than males (3.0%). OSFED was the commonest (3.5%), followed by bulimia nervosa (1.7%), anorexia nervosa (0.9%), binge eating disorder (0.6%) and ARFID (0.2%). Prevalence peaked at 17-19 years (13.9%). EDs were associated with lifetime self-harm (aOR 9.1 at 11-16; 4.4 at 17-25), SDQ-predicted probable disorder (aOR 14.7 at 11-16; 2.5 at 17-25), medication use (aOR 5.3) and mental health service contact (aOR 2.1). Conclusions: EDs are common among CYP in England and carry high levels of impairment, self-harm and comorbid mental health difficulties, particularly among 11-16-year-olds. Nonetheless, more than half of those meeting diagnostic criteria had no mental health service contact in the preceding year. Keywords: Eating disorders; prevalence; epidemiology; adolescence; ARFID; service use.

papers.title: Self-harm incidents and restrictive practice use in an acute female inpatient unit: a service evaluation of a continuous multi-system improvement approach
papers.abstract: BackgroundSelf-harm is a frequent and challenging occurrence in adult inpatient psychiatric units. The use of restrictive practice to manage self-harm incidents continues to be widespread within mental health environments despite increasing national and organisational guidance to minimise its use. Purpose/aimThe aim of this project was to introduce and evaluate a continuous quality improvement programme to progressively reduce incidents of self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. The project was set in a female acute mental health inpatient unit. The project sought to embed improvements in an inpatient units interventions, procedures, and culture and staffs mindset, and move towards a sustained collaborative and positive therapeutic and communication-based approach. MethodsA retrospective service evaluation design was employed to assess differences in the number of incidents of self-harm, enhanced observation, seclusion, restraint and rapid tranquillisation in the period following the introduction of a continuous whole-systems multimodal interventional initiative in 2019. Pre- and post-initiation data were compared (2017/18 compared to 2019/2025) to evaluate improvement and whether this had been sustained. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, and means. ResultsSelf-harm incidents reduced between 2017/18 and 2019, with a downward trend sustained between 2019 and 2025 (136 to 72 incidents respectively between 2019 and 2025; 47% reduction). A sustained reduction in the use of restrictive practice was shown in all domains pre- and post-initiation (2017/18 compared to 2025). Clinical implicationsNo one approach will successfully reduce self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. Approaches employed have to be multi-faceted, multi-interdisciplinary, collaborative, and blend together to deliver improvement. Sustained progress requires commitment to an iterative process of continuous collaboration, improvement and adaptation.

papers.title: Autistic Adults' Perceptions of the Adequacy of their Supports and Disability-Related Information: Instrument Validation & Preliminary Correlates
papers.abstract: Autistic adults face considerable challenges in receiving adequate support, from both paid/formal (such as from disability services) and unpaid/informal (for example, from friends and family) sources. Having adequate support can lead to better health and well-being outcomes. However, most instruments designed to assess adequacy of support were not made specifically for/with autistic adults. This paper presents a psychometric validation of the AASPIRE Adequacy of Supports and Information Scale (AASIS), a community-informed adaptation of a previously developed instrument (the Quality of Care and Support scale; Lucas-Carrasco et al., 2011), designed to be relevant and accessible to autistic adults. We also used the AASIS to explore correlates of perceptions of support in a sample of 798 autistic adults. Our confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure for the AASIS (factor one: Supports; factor two: Information). Further testing confirmed the instrument was invariant across several groups, including race/ethnicity, gender, intellectual disability, communication fluency, and self-versus proxy-report. Regression analyses suggested that the way in which participants joined the study (i.e., through community advertisements or via established healthcare/disability services) impacted whether they viewed their support as adequate. Additionally, a higher number of adverse childhood events and greater experience of discrimination were related to worse perceptions of support adequacy across both factors. Our findings support the preliminary validity of the AASIS across a variety of autistic people, though further testing is warranted. Findings also point to the importance of addressing the needs of autistic people who are minoritized and/or who have complex trauma histories.

papers.title: Patient-specific subnetwork connectivity predicts deep brain stimulation response in obsessive-compulsive disorder
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) can be an effective treatment for severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but response is variable, and objective, reliable predictors of who will respond positively are absent. In three individuals with OCD, we implanted intracranial electrodes across the cortico-striato-limbic network before DBS. Prefrontal gamma activity, most prominently in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), distinguished high-from low-symptom OCD states reproducibly across days. Acute stimulation of the ventral capsule/ventral striatum relieved OCD symptoms and, in one patient, significantly shifted this OFC gamma signal. Effective connectivity from therapeutic stimulation sites to these prefrontal regions defined three patient-specific OCD subnetworks; the baseline strength of the nucleus accumbens/ventral pallidum-OFC subnetwork predicted acute and long-term DBS response. Imaging-based modeling of current propagation in stimulation-activated ventral capsule to the OFC tracked acute response, suggesting that this prediction could be approximated from imaging alone. These findings outline a predictive, subnetwork-level framework for personalized DBS in OCD. HighlightsO_LIPrefrontal gamma encodes OCD symptom state and persists across recording days C_LIO_LIAcute VC/VS stimulation relieves symptoms and can shift the prefrontal gamma signal C_LIO_LIBaseline subnetwork connectivity predicts acute and long-term DBS response C_LIO_LIModeled ALIC-to-OFC tract activation approximates this prediction from imaging C_LI In BriefScangos and colleagues mapped three patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder with intracranial electrodes before deep brain stimulation. Prefrontal gamma activity tracked symptom state, and baseline connectivity from stimulation sites to these prefrontal regions predicted acute and long-term stimulation response. Modeled activation of ALIC-to-OFC tracts was associated with response, offering a route to this prediction from imaging alone. papers.title: Accentuated Divergence, Constrained Expression: Autistic Traits Modulate the Creative Brain in Adults with ADHD
papers.abstract: BackgroundAttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition, and co-occurring autistic traits may shape its phenotypic expression. Although creativity has been discussed as a relative strength in ADHD, it remains unclear whether autistic traits are associated with different dimensions of creativity in adults with ADHD and whether large-scale brain networks contribute to these associations. MethodsWe compared divergent thinking (DT) and real-life creativity between 65 adults with ADHD and 73 neurotypical controls. We used subgroup comparisons, partial correlation analyses, and multiple regression models to determine the effects of autistic traits (ATs) on creativity dimensions within the ADHD cohort. Guided by prior creativity-network research, we analyzed resting-state functional connectivity (FC) of the Default Mode Network (DMN) and Frontoparietal Network (FPN) to uncover the neural mechanisms. ResultsThe ADHD cohort demonstrated significantly higher scores on both DT (ps = 0.002-0.009) and real-life creativity measures (ps = 0.011-0.017) compared to the neurotypical control group. Importantly, increased ATs within the ADHD group were associated with a dissociated creativity profile, showing positive associations with DT but negative associations with real-life creativity. At the neural level, stronger right DMN-FPN connectivity mediated positive associations between ATs and DT performance (ps = 0.007-0.018), but mediated a negative association between ATs and self-reported imagination (p = 0.029). ConclusionsIn individuals with ADHD, co-occurring ATs exert a paradoxical effect on creativity, enhancing DT while compromising real-life creative achievement. In this subgroup with ADHD and elevated ATs, interventions should capitalize on ATs-associated ideational strengths while circumventing translational barriers, to enhance real-world creative outcomes.

papers.title: Intersectional inequalities in youth mental health measurement and outcomes: population-representative evidence from the UK Millennium Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPopulation-representative evidence on social inequalities in youth mental health from an intersectional perspective is limited. We investigated inequalities across multiple mental health outcomes among young adults and examined whether measures operated equivalently across social and intersectional groups. MethodsCross-sectional analyses were conducted with 9,675 participants aged 23 years from the nationally representative UK Millennium Cohort Study (born 2000-2002). Self-reported outcomes included psychological distress (Kessler-6), probable serious psychological distress/ caseness (Kessler-6 score [≥]13), psychological wellbeing (Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale; SWEMWBS), past-year self-harm, and lifetime suicide attempts. Measurement invariance analyses assessed comparability of the Kessler-6 and SWEMWBS across groups. Intersectional MAIHDA examined inequalities by sex assigned at birth, ethnic identity/background, sexual identity, and childhood poverty. Young people with lived experience of mental ill-health and/or social discrimination contributed to study design, interpretation, and reporting. FindingsLarge inequalities were observed across all outcomes, with the largest disparities by sexual identity, followed by sex assigned at birth, childhood poverty history, and ethnic identity/background. Across intersectional strata, predicted psychological distress ranged from-0.27 to 1.32 SDs, and psychological wellbeing from-0.54 to 0.11 SDs. Predicted prevalence varied 6.99-fold (9.81% to 68.55%) for psychological distress caseness, 6.84-fold (8.60% to 58.79%) for self-harm, and 22.10-fold (1.96% to 43.32%) for suicide attempts. Young people at the intersection of sexual minority status, female birth sex, childhood poverty, and some ethnic minority identities/backgrounds experienced particularly poor outcomes. Most inequalities showed cumulative patterns consistent with additive expectations, although some intersectional groups experienced better or worse outcomes than expected. Accounting for measurement differences revealed inequalities that were otherwise undetected. InterpretationFindings highlight the large extent of mental health inequalities when multiple dimensions of social (dis)advantage are considered, and the need to address both the social conditions generating these inequalities and the methodological assumptions shaping how they are measured and understood.

papers.title: Association of neurotransmitter-based polygenic scores with antidepressant treatment outcomes in patients with major depressive disorder
papers.abstract: Biologically informed polygenic scores (PGSs) may help interpret genetic associations with treatment outcomes. Here, we computed neurotransmitter-based PGSs (NeuroPGSs) for patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and assessed their association with SSRI treatment outcomes. By targeting genetic variants involved in key neurotransmission pathways, we developed PGSs for serotonergic (5228), gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA, 4103), dopaminergic (7061), and glutamatergic (5690) variants. We leveraged data from two cohorts of patients who received SSRIs for at least 4 weeks: the International SSRI Pharmacogenomics Consortium (ISPC) and the Pharmacogenomics Research Network Antidepressants Medication Pharmacogenomics Study (PGRN-AMPS). Treatment response was defined as [≥]50% reduction from baseline depression symptoms, measured using 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD-17) in ISPC and 16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (QIDS-C16) in PGRN-AMPS. Remission was defined as HRSD-17 [≤]7 (ISPC) or QIDS-C16[≤]5 (PGRN-AMPS). The association between each NeuroPGS and antidepressant response or remission was evaluated using logistic regression models, adjusting for age, sex and five genetic principal components, with statistical significance determined at Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p<0.05. The GABAergic-based PGS was associated with SSRI response (aOR per SD = 1.45, 95%CI: 1.14-1.85). Patients with the highest GABAergic PGS (10th decile) had 2.59-fold higher odds of response (95%CI: 1.46-4.60) compared to those with the lowest decile (1st decile). These exploratory findings support further evaluation of NeuroPGSs; independent replication and assessment of incremental predictive value are needed before clinical application.

papers.title: Event-related potential signatures of auditory predictive processing in first-episode psychosis: a passive pattern-based study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPredictive-processing accounts propose altered prediction-error signaling in psychosis. However, event-related potential (ERP) findings in first-episode psychosis (FEP) are inconsistent and focused predominantly on mismatch negativity (MMN). Examining anticipatory and later post-stimulus ERP responses alongside MMN within a single passive paradigm may broaden the assessment of predictive processing in FEP. Methods34 participants with non-affective FEP and 34 healthy controls (HC) underwent EEG during a passive auditory pattern-based paradigm. Mean amplitudes of contingent negative variation (CNV), MMN, and post-imperative negative variation (PINV) were quantified at five frontocentral electrodes. Exploratory analyses examined N1 and P2 mean amplitudes. Mixed models tested group, electrode, and group-by-electrode effects adjusting for age, sex and years of education. Regressions examined ERP associations with psychotic-like experiences, neurocognition, and social cognition across groups, and with symptoms, functioning, and antipsychotic dose within FEP. ResultsFEP participants reported more psychotic-like experiences and showed poorer global and social cognition than HC (all p-FDR [≤].042). Standardized adjusted FEP-HC differences at FCz were nonsignificant for CNV ({beta} = -0.46), MMN ({beta} = -0.30), and PINV ({beta} = -0.10; all p-FDR [≥].265). Exploratory analyses identified lower P2 amplitude in FEP at FCz ({beta} = -0.73; p-FDR =.019) and in the averaged frontocentral ROI ({beta} = -0.64; p-FDR =.027). No ERP-phenotype associations survived FDR correction. ConclusionsDespite phenotypic differences between FEP and HC, no significant differences emerged in the primary ERP indices of predictive processing examined. The exploratory P2 finding and its possible relationship to predictive processing and frontal dysfunction in FEP warrant further investigation.

papers.title: Focus or Feeding: A Quantitative Analysis of Prescribed Amphetamines in Human Milk
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAmphetamine (AMP) and its derivates are commonly prescribed for the management of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This study aimed to 1) quantify AMPs transfer into human milk in lactating women receiving therapeutic doses and 2) contextualize infant exposure. MethodsMilk samples and dyad health histories of thirteen lactating women treated with varying doses of either mixed AMP, dextroamphetamine, or lisdexamfetamine were released for this study from the InfantRisk Human Milk Biorepository. Milk drug concentrations were quantified by validated liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and used to calculate standard relative infant dose (RIDmat) and RID standardized to the defined daily dose (RIDDDD) of 15 mg AMP base. ResultsAverage milk concentrations (Cavg) of AMP base ranged from 23.3 to 297.0 ng/mL and increased linearly (R{superscript 2} = 0.92) with maternal daily dose. The RIDmat ranged 3.6-10.8% and RIDDDD ranged 1.4-21.8%. The fitted regression line crossed the 10% RIDDDD threshold at 1.17x DDD, with the upper 95% prediction limit crossing at 0.84x DDD. No adverse event reported by the mother-infant dyads were attributed to AMP exposure, notably including absence of reduced milk supply. ConclusionsThe levels of AMP observed in human milk followed a dose predictable manner. The average patient was predicted to remain below the 10% RID DDD safety threshold at total daily doses at or below approximately 28 mg of mixed AMP salts or 59 mg of lisdexamfetamine. Ninety-five percent of patients were predicted to remain below the threshold at or below approximately 20 mg and 40 mg, respectively.

papers.title: Shared Social Brain Gray Matter Reductions in Depression, Schizophrenia, and Alcohol Use Disorder: A Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: ImportanceAnhedonia, social withdrawal and executive deficits represent transdiagnostic symptoms in depression, schizophrenia and addition, yet transdiagnostic brain volumetric alterations and their contribution to these symptom domains have not been systematically characterized. ObjectiveTo determine common and disorder-specific gray matter deficits in patients with schizophrenia (SZ), major depression disorder (MDD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) compared to heathy controls. Data SourcesA comprehensive literature search using three databases including PubMed, Web of Science and PsycInfo (between January 2000 to March 2024) as well as searches on review articles. Study SelectionStudies had to be published in English, reporting whole-brain results, comparing patients and healthy controls. Data Extraction and SynthesisThis meta-analysis adhered to the PRISMA guidelines and was pre-registered (https://osf.io/s57uq) prior to data analysis. Data was independently extracted and verified by 3 contributors, and statistical brain maps were generated using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images (SDM-PSI) random-effects model. 147 VBM studies encompassing 90 Schizophrenia, 44 MDD and 13 AUD studies were finally included. Main Outcomes and MeasuresStatistical maps of common and disorder-specific gray matter deficits in patients versus healthy controls are presented. Statistical inference utilized permutation tests, with threshold at p < .0025 and cluster extent of 10 voxels. Heterogeneity was evaluated using the I2 statistic and publication bias using Eggers regression test. ResultsCapitalizing on a coordinate-based meta-analysis involving n=13,041 participants, we found shared GMV alterations in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, ventral anterior cingulate cortex, insula, superior temporal gyrus. On the network level, we found robust functional interactions of the identified shared regions with the cortical midline structures as well as social and theory of mind-related behavioral functions. Subsequent characterization analyses highlighted the involvement of dopaminergic and serotonergic neurotransmitters as well as associated genetic annotations. Conclusions and RelevanceOverall, the present meta-analysis found common as well as separate GMV abnormalities in schizophrenia, major depressive disorder and alcohol use disorder suggesting a common neurostructural substrate and treatment target for social withdrawal and anhedonia across these disorders. Key pointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSCan transdiagnostic meta-analytic mapping identify common gray matter alterations associated with shared reward-related, social, and executive symptoms across major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, and alcohol use disorder? FindingsThe meta-analysis determined transdiagnostic gray matter volume reductions in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, ventral anterior cingulate cortex, insula, superior temporal gyrus. We found robust functional interactions of these regions with cortical midline structures including social and theory of mind related functions, while transcriptomic characterization highlighted the involvement of neurotransmitter systems and shared genetic markers. MeaningThe study demonstrates regional-specific transdiagnostic brain structural alterations that may mediate social dysfunction and anhedonia across disorders.

papers.title: Promoting Community Living and Participation Outcomes Among Young Autistic Adults: Promising Results for an Autistic-Delivered Peer Support Intervention
papers.abstract: Autistic young adults experience substantial gaps in services supporting community living and participation. The Community Autism Peer Support (CAPS) program is a community-based intervention in which trained autistic peer specialists provide individualized support to autistic young adults pursuing self-determined goals related to community participation and independent living. We conducted a single-site, two-arm randomized controlled trial to evaluate the feasibility of implementing the CAPS program. Forty autistic adults aged 18-30 years were randomized to CAPS (n = 20) or services as usual alone (n = 20) and assessed at baseline, 3 months, and 12 months. Study findings showed that CAPS attracted autistic young adults with diverse demographic and diagnostic backgrounds, and most intervention participants remained engaged in services for extended periods. While the study was underpowered to detect statistical differences in outcomes because it was not a main focus of the research, a consistent pattern of results favored the CAPS condition across all outcomes. The largest positive signals were observed for overall and social quality of life, with additional favorable changes in internalized stigma, unmet needs, social functioning, loneliness, and positive autistic identity. Findings provide support for the feasibility and promise of an autistic-delivered peer specialist model focused on community living and participation. The consistent pattern of favorable changes supports continued development of CAPS as a person-centered approach to addressing outcomes important to autistic adults.

papers.title: Title Mapping the brain signature of dyslexia risk onto histamine, acetylcholine and glutamate receptor systems
papers.abstract: The brain differences of dyslexia are well described and its genetic risk is now measurable; the brain systems that connect the two are unknown. That link decides which measures complement one another in early identification and which systems intervention research should examine. Here we compared large-scale polygenic score maps of brain structure in dyslexia with normative maps of brain neurotransmitter systems. The structural signature of genetic liability aligned with the cortical distribution of neurotransmitter systems. The strongest and most consistent alignment appeared for the histamine H3 receptor, the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor. The alignment was most pronounced in cingulate, medial and superior frontal cortex and the paracentral lobule. The H3 alignment held after adjustment for cortical position and for metabolic and cognitive reference maps. Once the component common to all nineteen maps and position were removed together, no individual system remained significant, while the shared component itself aligned with liability. The signature therefore follows the topography these systems share. In 169 children, per-person alignment with the H3 map related to reading skill with the opposite sign to liability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to relate the structural signature of genetic liability for dyslexia to normative maps of neurotransmitter receptor and transporter density. It places that signature within the shared geography of the systems that set attention, arousal and synaptic plasticity during learning, and gives the genetics of dyslexia a testable biological axis.

papers.title: Dysfunctional Sleep Beliefs and Attitudes in Major Depressive Disorder: Dimensional Associations with Clinical Phenotypes and Gut-Neuroimmune-Metabolic-Oxidative Pathways
papers.abstract: BackgroundInsomnia is highly prevalent in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the clinical and biological significance of dysfunctional beliefs and attitudes about sleep (DBAS) in MDD remains poorly understood. We examined whether distinct DBAS dimensions are associated with insomnia severity, depressive phenotypes, and neuroimmune-metabolic-oxidative (NIMETOX) biomarkers. MethodsDBAS-30 dimensions, clinical phenotypes, and NIMETOX biomarkers were assessed in 87 hospitalized patients with MDD and 31 healthy controls. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to ascertain DBAS cognitive dimensions, and associations were examined using multivariable analyses. ResultsCompared with controls, MDD patients showed lower scores on "perceived consequences of insomnia," "sleep-related worry and helplessness," and "medication-related beliefs," but higher "causal attributions to aging or biochemical imbalance" scores. A composite DBAS score reflecting these 4 MDD-associated cognitive dimensions was constructed, labeled DBAS dimensional index (DBAS-DI). This score was lower in MDD and inversely associated with Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores, overall MDD severity, physiosomatic symptoms, current suicidal ideation, and recurrence of illness. DBAS-DI and the expectations domain jointly explained 35.4% of the variance in ISI scores, with inverse and positive associations, respectively. The DBAS-DI score was inversely associated with indices of the acute-phase inflammatory response, oxidative stress, fecal branched-chain short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and positively associated with serum antioxidant capacity and protective SCFAs, such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate. ConclusionsDBAS abnormalities in MDD extend beyond insomnia-related cognitions and are associated with illness severity, suicidality, recurrence, and NIMETOX alterations. These findings suggest that dysfunctional sleep-related cognitions are embedded within broader immune-oxidative and gut microbial-metabolic processes that may contribute to the insomnia-depression interface.

papers.title: Genetically regulated molecular mediators of phenotypic heterogeneity in autism spectrum disorder
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows wide phenotypic variation, from adults without intellectual disability and with low support needs to minimally verbal children with intellectual disability and severe behavioral symptoms. Genetic studies of this heterogeneity have focused mainly on high-impact de novo variants and polygenic scores; here we investigate, at the molecular level, the role of common variants. Materials and methodsWe analyzed genotypic and phenotypic data from 9,332 individuals with ASD in the SPARK cohort. We considered 31 traits: six latent factors derived from the Social Communication Questionnaire and the Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised, 22 co-occurring diagnoses, parent-reported IQ range, age at diagnosis, and age at first walking. We performed within-case genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and, for the 10 traits with evidence of SNP heritability, association analyses with genetically predicted gene and protein expression, splicing, and enhancer activity in brain and blood (xWAS). Nominated genes were tested for enrichment in biological processes, brain cell types, and developmental stages. xWAS-derived transcriptional signatures were compared with chemical perturbation signatures from CMap/LINCS L1000 to prioritize candidate drugs. ResultsGWAS identified seven genome-wide significant loci for five traits, including loci near GABRG3 and TENM2 associated with co-occurring sleep, feeding or toileting problems. xWAS identified seven gene-trait associations involving three phenotypes (FDR < 0.1), including CACNA1G with communication skills and NEGR1 with learning disability. GWAS and xWAS nominated different genes which however converged on synaptic transmission and gated channel activity, with preferential expression in neurons during later stages of brain development. PARP and p38 MAPK inhibitors were predicted to reverse the signatures of both social-communication and repetitive-behavior phenotypes, whereas several compound classes, including histone deacetylase inhibitors and mTOR inhibitors, were predicted to reverse the signatures of some phenotypes while mimicking those of others. ConclusionCombining within-case GWAS with xWAS nominates candidate genes mediating common-variant effects on ASD heterogeneity, provides biological insight, and suggests candidates for phenotypically stratified drug repositioning.

papers.title: Individual-level Structural Neuroimaging Biomarkers across the Psychosis Spectrum
papers.abstract: Background and HypothesisAlthough psychotic disorders are characterized by widespread cortical thinning, translating these findings into individualized biomarkers remains challenging. Regional Vulnerability Index (RVI) and Neuroscore are candidate individual-level biomarkers that quantify the similarity between an individuals structural brain pattern and generic psychosis-associated alterations. This study investigated cortical thickness (CT)-based RVI and Neuroscore, along with mean CT deviation from healthy individuals, across the psychosis spectrum. Study DesignUsing structural 3T MRI data from 289 participants (clinical high risk for psychosis [CHR], n=39; first episode psychosis [FEP], n=44, chronic psychosis [CP], n=86; healthy controls [HC], n=120), RVI, Neuroscore, and mean CT deviation (z) scores were computed from region-wise CT measures quantified using FreeSurfer v7.2. Group differences and associations with symptoms were evaluated. Study ResultsRVI and Neuroscore were significantly higher, and mean CT z-scores lower, in FEP and CP compared with CHR and HC, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (|Cohens d| = 0.55-1.15). No differences were observed between FEP and CP or CHR and HC. Indices were not associated with psychosis-spectrum symptom severity in the CHR, FEP, or CP groups. RVI (r = -0.561, p < .001) and Neuroscore (r = -0.997, p < .001) were strongly negatively correlated with the mean CT z-score. ConclusionsCT-based RVI and Neuroscore appear to index established disease status but not risk status, while showing substantial overlap with mean CT deviation. These findings highlight the need to further refine these biomarkers through data-driven and multimodal approaches to improve their utility for risk and prognostic prediction.

papers.title: Average accuracy hides where a brain-imaging psychosis risk model fails across clinical cohorts
papers.abstract: Brain-imaging models predicting psychiatric outcomes are rarely tested where they would be used. Clinical high risk for psychosis is a demanding test case because services differ in whom they recruit and how they record transition. We re-estimated a published structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) risk model and applied it unchanged to four independent cohorts (685 participants, 106 transitions). Discrimination was weak (area under the curve, 0.56) and near chance in the two cohorts not previously used to evaluate the model (0.53 and 0.56). Predicted risks did not transfer (calibration slope, 0.17). Exploratory performance landscapes, which map local discrimination across participant characteristics, showed that discrimination varied with negative-symptom severity, also in external cohorts, whereas apparent age- and brain-age-related variation depended on single cohorts; no global test survived multiple-testing correction. Reporting where a model works, not only its average accuracy, can reveal when one diagnostic label hides several prediction problems.

papers.title: Spectral power and functional connectivity of resting EEG in people exposed to armed conflict and controls
papers.abstract: Exposure to armed conflict can leave persistent effects on mental health, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly characterized, particularly in populations exposed to prolonged violence outside narrowly defined post traumatic stress disorder samples. Here we examined resting state electroencephalographic activity in 122 Colombian adults, including 74 participants exposed to armed conflict and 48 controls. Eyes closed EEG was analysed for 240 seconds per participant. We quantified absolute and relative spectral power across delta, theta, alpha and beta bands and regional functional connectivity using weighted phase lag index in theta, alpha and beta. Group comparisons were adjusted for age, education, sex and assessment year, with correction across 78 EEG contrasts. Median occipital and global alpha power was lower in exposed participants, although adjusted estimates were close to the null and confidence intervals were broad. Temporal theta relative power was lower in exposed participants at nominal significance, but this association did not survive Holm correction. No spectral power or regional connectivity contrast remained significant after multiple testing correction. Exploratory associations between EEG measures and MoCA performance were modest in participants with confirmed scores. These findings provide a systematic characterization of resting EEG after exposure to armed conflict in a population shaped by prolonged violence and displacement. They also indicate that large or widespread alterations in resting spectral power and connectivity were not detectable with the current sample and analytical framework, while defining candidate signals and methodological priorities for larger studies of conflict related brain health.

papers.title: From Gut to Brain: A Longitudinal Assessment of Intestinal Permeability and Immune Activation Markers in Early-Stage Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorders
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) have been linked to immune dysregulation and altered intestinal barrier function, although findings across studies remain inconsistent. The present study investigated circulating markers of intestinal permeability and immune activation in individuals with early-stage SSD and healthy controls and examined their associations with clinical outcomes. Serum concentrations of intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (iFABP), zonulin, soluble CD14 (sCD14), bactericidal/permeability-increasing protein (BPI), and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) were measured in 36 patients with SSD at baseline and one-year follow-up and in 36 matched healthy controls. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI) were used to evaluate group differences and longitudinal changes. No biomarker differences between patients and controls, and no longitudinal changes within patients, remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. Similarly, biomarker concentrations were not associated with symptom severity, global functioning, or neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR). Exploratory analyses identified a robust positive association between BMI and zonulin concentrations and additional associations among iFABP, LBP, and sCD14. Exploratory mixed-effects models identified a negative non-significant association between iFABP and sCD14 after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI. Overall, the findings do not support a generalized alteration of gut permeability or immune activation markers in SSD. Instead, they suggest that variation in gut-related biomarkers may be more strongly influenced by metabolic and individual factors than by diagnosis or current symptom severity.

papers.title: Effects of Cannabidiol on Auditory Mismatch Negativity in Autistic Children
papers.abstract: Pharmacological treatments targeting core autistic features remain limited. In neurotypical adults, cannabidiol (CBD) alters mismatch negativity (MMN), an electrophysiological marker of automatic auditory deviance detection that has been associated with autistic traits. The effects of CBD on MMN, as measured using electroencephalography (EEG), in autistic children remain unknown. This secondary analysis of a pilot randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial examined the effects of 12 weeks of oral CBD oil on MMN during a duration-deviant auditory oddball task. We hypothesised that CBD would produce more negative MMN amplitudes and shorter peak latencies relative to placebo. Nineteen autistic children (6-12 years, 8 female) received CBD (dose) and placebo in randomised order, separated by an 8-week washout. Age-adjusted linear mixed-effects models tested Time (baseline, follow-up) x Treatment (CBD, placebo) effects on mean MMN amplitude and peak latency separately at Fz and FCz. Exploratory Spearman correlations examined baseline associations between MMN and Developmental Behaviour Checklist-2 (DBC-2) Social Relating scores. At FCz, latency decreased following CBD but increased following placebo but did not survive FDR correction (p = .029, pFDR = .058) and no other interactions were significant. Higher baseline DBC-2 Social Relating scores were associated with more negative MMN amplitude at FCz ({rho} = -.58, pFDR = .028) and Fz ({rho} = -.59, pFDR = .028). These findings provide tentative evidence that CBD may modulate MMN latency in autistic children. Larger trials should clarify CBDs effects on MMN and further examine the association between MMN amplitude and social-relating difficulties.

papers.title: Why are girls more distressed than boys? A multi-domain framework applied to longitudinal data across four countries
papers.abstract: BackgroundGirls are more likely than boys to experience psychological distress during adolescence. Drivers of this gender gap remain under-studied, despite its large impact on later life and outcomes, especially for women. Explanatory factors can be gendered in their prevalence (differential exposure) and/or in their impact (differential susceptibility). We developed a multi-domain framework of explanatory factors for distress and applied it in four low- and middle-income countries. MethodsWe first proposed a framework of explanatory factors for psychological distress grouped into seven domains (biological, cognitive, psychological, behavioural, social, environmental and broader societal). We applied this framework to identify explanatory variables assessed in childhood and adolescence in the Young Lives longitudinal cohort studies in Ethiopia (N=908), India (N=952), Peru (N=634) and Vietnam (N=887). Distress symptoms at 18-19 years were measured with the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire Emotional Symptoms scale. Gendered prevalence of each explanatory factor was tested with Mann-Whitney tests, and gendered impact with country-specific linear regressions including a gender-by-factor interaction term. Exploratory boosted-tree machine-learning models, interpreted with SHAP values and permutation feature importance, examined the contribution of these factors to the gender gap in each country. ResultsDistress was higher in girls than boys in every country, the gap ranging from 0.62 points in Ethiopia and Vietnam to 1.76 in India and 2.45 in Peru. Some explanatory factors were consistently gendered in prevalence (e.g. girls experienced greater role overload in each country), while others were gendered only in some countries (e.g. study amount was higher for girls in Peru and Vietnam, but not Ethiopia or India). Gendered impacts on distress displayed more variability across countries. For example, higher self-esteem was more protective for boys than girls in India, Peru and Vietnam, but more protective for girls in Ethiopia. The machine-learning models identified important predictors across all framework domains, though their salience varied by country. ConclusionsOur findings underscore the importance of considering multi-domain explanations for mental-health outcomes and observed inequalities in mental health. Large cross-country differences in the gender gap and in the prevalence and influence of explanatory factors caution against generalising drivers of mental-health outcomes and inequalities across contexts.

papers.title: Psychometric Properties of the Short-Form Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ-15) in Medical Sciences Students: A Cross-Cultural Validation Study with Diagnostic Utility Analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveMindfulness is a robust predictor of mental health, yet the psychometric properties of the short-form Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ-15) have not been examined in Iranian populations. This study evaluated the psychometric properties, factor structure, and diagnostic utility of the FFMQ-15 among medical sciences students. ParticipantsA total of 348 students (178 females, 170 males) from Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences participated. MethodsParticipants completed the FFMQ-15, Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ), Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), and Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ). Data were analyzed using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, composite reliability, and ROC curve analysis. ResultsBoth EFA and CFA supported the five-factor model, revealing a culturally unique item loading pattern. The FFMQ-15 demonstrated strong convergent and discriminant validity. ROC analysis indicated acceptable diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing high- and low-worry groups (AUC = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.66-0.78). ConclusionsThe FFMQ-15 demonstrated acceptable psychometric properties in Iranian medical students. The non-reactivity facet exhibited cultural variability, suggesting that cross-cultural adaptation is essential. The instrument shows promise for screening in high-stress educational settings.

papers.title: Neighborhood socioeconomic status and environmental burden show diverging associations with cognitive impairment in community-dwelling older adults
papers.abstract: STRUCTURED ABSTRACTO_ST_ABSOBJECTIVEC_ST_ABSResearch on neighborhood context and cognitive health often relies on composite indices that collapse neighborhood socioeconomic status (SES) and aspects of the built environment into a single score. This study examined the extent to which neighborhood SES and built environment were associated with late-life cognitive impairment. METHODParticipants were 281 predominantly Black older adults who completed the Self-Administered Gerocognitive Exam (SAGE), a brief cognitive screening measure. Participants also provided their home address to obtain four neighborhood metrics: Two composite measures of neighborhood disadvantage, the Environmental Justice Index (EJI) and the EJI Social-Environmental Rank, as well as the EJI Social Vulnerability Rank as a measure of neighborhood SES, and the EJI Environmental Burden Rank to measure exposure to hazardous aspects of the built environment. RESULTSLower neighborhood SES was associated with higher odds of cognitive impairment. In contrast, greater environmental burden was associated with lower odds of impairment, with years of education as a moderator; the association was strongest among individuals with high levels of education. The two composite scores were not associated with cognitive impairment. CONCLUSIONComposite measures of neighborhood features may obscure distinct pathways of their effects on cognition.

papers.title: Attenuated GlycoRNA-microglial transcriptional coupling in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of patients with major depressive disorder: an exploratory interaction-based in-silico analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundGlycosylated RNAs (GlycoRNAs) participate in immune recognition and intercellular communication1, but their relationship with brain cell-type transcriptional signatures in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains unclear. We examined GlycoRNA-related transcriptional coupling with microglial and other cellular signatures in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). MethodPostmortem DLPFC transcriptomic data from 22 controls and 26 MDD patients (GSE102556)2 were analyzed. GlycoRNA-related pathway enrichment was quantified using gene set variation analysis (GSVA)3, whereas microglial, neuronal, astrocytic, and oligodendrocytic signatures were derived using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA)4-6. Pearson correlations, linear regression, and generalized estimating equations (GEE) evaluated cell-type-specific associations and diagnostic interactions. Exploratory GEE results underwent false discovery rate (FDR) correction. ResultsNo differentially expressed genes survived FDR correction, and GlycoRNA-related and cell-type signatures did not differ significantly between groups. In controls, GlycoRNA enrichment was positively associated with the microglial signature ({beta} = 0.447, FDR-P = 0.006), with significantly weaker associations for neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes (all FDR-P < 0.05). The two-way GlycoRNA x is_microglia interaction was nominally significant ({beta} = 0.210, P = 0.048), confirming that GlycoRNA transcriptional coupling is substantially stronger for microglia than for the other three cell types combined. The microglial association was numerically attenuated in MDD ({beta} difference = -0.273, P = 0.167), but diagnostic interactions were nonsignificant. ConclusionsGlycoRNA pathway transcriptional enrichment exhibits preferential microglial association in control DLPFC. Its possible attenuation in MDD remains.

papers.title: Baseline Response Criterion and Changes in Emotional Bias as Markers of Esketamine Response in Treatment-Resistant Depression
papers.abstract: Negative emotional bias, including reduced processing of positive information and negative interpretation of ambiguous stimuli, is a core feature of depression. Esketamine, an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist with rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), reduces depressive symptoms, but its effects on distinct components of emotional processing remain unclear. Fifty-three patients with TRD and 53 healthy controls performed an Emotional Facial Expression Morphing task. Patients were assessed at baseline, 24 hours after the first esketamine administration, and after 4 weeks of treatment. Statistical models examined detection thresholds for happy and sad faces, negative categorisation of neutral faces, and signal detection indices separating emotion-neutral discrimination sensitivity (d') from response criterion (c), indexing the evidence required to report the presence of an emotion. At baseline, patients required greater happy-face intensity for emotion detection and were more likely to categorise detected neutral faces as negative. They also showed a more conservative response criterion without group difference in discrimination sensitivity. Responders showed an early increase in d' and, by week 4, less negative categorisation of neutral faces than non-responders. A lower baseline response criterion was associated with responder status and, in secondary continuous analyses, with greater subsequent MADRS improvement. These findings indicate that TRD involves abnormalities across detection-related, valence-related, and decisional aspects of facial-emotion processing that are differently associated with esketamine response: baseline response criterion emerged as a candidate prognostic marker, whereas negative categorisation of neutral faces tracked clinical response. Assessing these domains may inform clinical evaluation, pending independent replication.

papers.title: Evaluating 5-Item Short Forms of Youth Depression Measures
papers.abstract: Brief assessments reduce clinician and patient burden and increase utilization. Recently, five core depression symptoms (low mood, poor concentration, low self-worth, loss of interest, low energy) have been shown to be particularly sensitive to treatment effects in adults. How these core depressive symptom domains perform for screening or diagnostic purposes in youth is unknown. To address this question, we extracted five analogous symptom items from four widely used symptom assessment tools for children and adolescents (Child Behavior Checklist [CBCL], Youth Self Report [YSR], Parent General Behavior Inventory [P-GBI], and Adolescent General Behavior Inventory [A-GBI]) to create 5-item short forms. We evaluated their psychometric properties and diagnostic utility in a large (N=1185), racially diverse sample (48% Black youth) across community and academic outpatient mental health settings, with diagnoses established through LEAD consensus. All short forms correlated highly with full-length measures (r=.74-.92) and demonstrated comparable inter-item correlations (r =.19-.46). The short forms did not differ meaningfully from the full measures in correlations with psychiatric diagnoses, demographics, or diagnostic interviews. Area under the curve (AUC) values for identifying depression and any mood disorder diagnosis (determined by semi-structured diagnostic interviews) were fair to good (AUC=0.60-0.79), which were not worse than full measures, except for the P-GBI. The CBCL-5, YSR-5, P-GBI-5, and A-GBI-5 may be useful brief depression assessments in youth. How these five symptom domains perform as outcome measures in treatment deserves study.

papers.title: An Imaging Risk Score for Bipolar Disorder: Multimodal Comparison and Integration with Polygenic Risk
papers.abstract: BackgroundBiological risk scores provide objective markers of bipolar disorder (BD) liability. Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have led to polygenic risk scores (PRSs) that capture genetic liability to BD at the individual level. We lack a comparable large-scale effort to leverage a brain-wide association study (BWAS) to create an imaging risk score (IRS) that captures brain structural liability to BD at the individual-level. Here, we conduct the largest multivariate BWAS of BD and develop a BD IRS. We compare the BD IRS to the PRS and assess their combined predictive performance in multimodal risk score (MRS) models. MethodsOur multivariate BD BWAS used 153 structural neuroimaging features from 3902 cases and 6855 controls (mean age (sd)=35.47 years (13.42), 56.70% female) in a cross-validated machine learning approach. Using the resulting model coefficients, we constructed an IRS. We then evaluated the out-of-sample performance of the IRS, PRS derived from the largest GWAS to date, and combined MRS model using logistic regression in a subset of individuals with imaging and genetic data (nBD=486, ncontrols=1701, age (sd)=33.10 (12.02), 56.47% female). We also performed stratified analyses for demographic and BD clinical groups. Prediction performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Subsequent analyses examined associations between each risk score and BD relevant symptoms in developing youth. OutcomesIn predicting case status, the BD BWAS model achieved a mean AUCBD of 0.62 (sdBD=0.08) and in stratified analyses, had higher prediction than subgroup-specific BWAS models. The BD type II BWAS was the only exception (AUCBDII=0.60, sdBDII=0.07 vs AUCBD=0.58, sdBD=0.09). The BD PRS had an AUCBD of 0.65 (CI95%=0.63-0.68) and a higher AUC than subtype-specific PRS in stratified analyses. The PRS typically attained a higher AUC than the IRS. Notably, the IRS and PRS were uncorrelated (r=0.03, p=0.11). MRS models outperformed the prediction of individual PRS and IRS with the strongest prediction for BD type I (AUCBD=0.74, CI95%=0.70-0.78). The IRS had the strongest associations with BD-related symptoms in developing youth including increased energy (OR=1.21, pfdr=0.03) and distress from psychotic-like experiences (OR=1.23, pfdr=0.04). InterpretationOur BD IRS is a novel biological indicator of BD risk. The lack of correlation between the IRS and PRS along with improved MRS prediction suggests the two risk scores capture some orthogonal liability to BD. We show that integrating imaging and genetics is useful for biological characterization of BD and should be considered for the development of clinically relevant prediction models.
